column2: Exoplanets, planets outside our solar system, have transformed our view of the universe. Since the discovery of 51 Pegasi b in 1995, astronomers have cataloged thousands of worlds that defy the imagination: gas giants orbiting so close to their stars that their atmospheres boil away, planets covered by endless oceans, and Earth-sized worlds in zones where liquid water, and perhaps even life, could exist. Some orbit stars as close as Proxima Centauri, while others lie hundreds of light-years away. Most fascinating of all, many of these worlds look nothing like those of the solar system, which suggests that the planetary diversity of the cosmos is even richer than we had dreamed. In the coming decades, missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope and new ground-based observatories may help us detect not only exotic atmospheres but also chemical signatures of life on distant planets.

TRAPPIST-1 is a star system about 40 light-years away in Aquarius, made up of an ultracool dwarf star and seven Earth-sized exoplanets, three of which, TRAPPIST-1e, f and g, lie in the habitable zone. The system has drawn great scientific interest because it could host planets with liquid water, and some might even hold more water than Earth. Recent observations with the James Webb Space Telescope are looking for atmospheres and possible biosignatures, making TRAPPIST-1 one of the best candidates in the search for life beyond the solar system.

Planet in the habitable zone with water vapor detected in its atmosphere. K2-18b is an exoplanet 124 light-years from Earth, in Leo, that has caught the attention of the scientific community for its potential habitability. This world, about 2.6 times the size of Earth, orbits within the habitable zone of its star, which means it could have liquid water on its surface. Recent observations with the James Webb Space Telescope have revealed carbon-bearing molecules such as methane and carbon dioxide in its atmosphere. Possible signs of dimethyl sulfide (DMS) have also been detected, a compound that on Earth is produced mainly by living organisms, especially marine phytoplankton. Although these findings are promising, scientists urge caution, since detecting a single possible biosignature is not conclusive proof of life. More observations and studies are needed to confirm these hints and rule out non-biological explanations. The interest in K2-18b comes from its classification as a possible "Hycean planet", a kind of world with liquid oceans and a hydrogen-rich atmosphere, conditions that could favor life as we know it. This discovery is a significant step in the search for life beyond our solar system and highlights the importance of future missions to explore and better understand these distant worlds.
